prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff passenger.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that the Montreal Convention's two-year limitations period is a condition precedent to suit that may nonetheless be affected by equitable considerations, or alternatively the airline's bankruptcy stay tolls it.

Cite at least six decisions of the Eleventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

Before you cite anything, call find_authority with the proposition and the circuit: it returns real cases that courts have cited for it, in the courts' own words, and that circuit's own F.3d opinions saying so. Cite from those results rather than from memory.
answer:
## ARGUMENT†

**The Montreal Convention's two-year period does not foreclose equitable relief; alternatively, 11 U.S.C. § 108(c) extended it.**

### A. The "condition precedent" label does not end the inquiry.

Article 35(1) provides that the right to damages "shall be extinguished" if an action is not brought within two years. Article 35(2) provides that "[t]he method of calculating that period shall be determined by the law of the court seised of the case." "The interpretation of a treaty, like the interpretation of a statute, begins with its text." *Lindo v. NCL (Bahamas), Ltd.*, 652 F.3d 1257, 1275 (11th Cir. 2011) (quotation omitted); *see United States v. Duarte-Acero*, 208 F.3d 1282, 1285 (11th Cir. 2000). Paragraph 1 fixes the period's length and consequence; paragraph 2 commits its calculation to forum law. Deciding which days count, including whether circumstances suspend the count, is part of calculating the period.

Calling the period a condition precedent does not answer what forum law may count. This Court examines a time provision's text, history, and statutory setting before assigning it consequences. *See Pugh v. Brook (In re Pugh)*, 158 F.3d 530, 533–38 (11th Cir. 1998) (treating a bankruptcy time limit as a waivable statute of limitations rather than a jurisdictional bar). Appellant is aware of no published decision of this Court deciding whether equitable considerations may affect Article 35. *Marotte v. American Airlines, Inc.*, 296 F.3d 1255, 1259 (11th Cir. 2002), applied the predecessor Warsaw Convention to a passenger's claims but should not be read to resolve that question.

Contrary authority is distinguishable or should not be followed. *Fishman v. Delta Air Lines, Inc.*, 132 F.3d 138, 143–45 (2d Cir. 1998), held that the Warsaw Convention's two-year bar was not tolled for a passenger's infancy, relying in part on drafting history. It arose under a different treaty, does not bind this Court, and addressed a disability rather than an external legal barrier or carrier misconduct. *Lozano v. Montoya Alvarez*, 572 U.S. 1, 10–15 (2014), declined to presume that equitable tolling applies to a Hague Convention period, emphasizing the signatories' shared expectations and that the provision was not a statute of limitations. Appellant therefore does not rest on the domestic presumption alone. Article 35, unlike the provision in *Lozano*, bars the damages remedy and expressly refers calculation to forum law.

### B. The circumstances warrant equitable relief.

Where forum law applies, equitable tolling reaches extraordinary circumstances beyond the plaintiff's control and unavoidable even with diligence. *Arce v. Garcia*, 434 F.3d 1254, 1261 (11th Cir. 2006). The plaintiff must show both diligent pursuit of rights and an extraordinary circumstance that stood in the way. *Downs v. McNeil*, 520 F.3d 1311, 1319 (11th Cir. 2008). Relief is "to be applied sparingly," *Jackson v. Astrue*, 506 F.3d 1349, 1353 (11th Cir. 2007) (quotation omitted), and is unavailable to one who fails to act diligently, *Drew v. Department of Corrections*, 297 F.3d 1278, 1286–88 (11th Cir. 2002).

Appellant satisfies that demanding standard. [Plead record facts, with citations: diligence before and after the deadline; the bankruptcy stay; any carrier representations or conduct that induced delay.] A court order or statute forbidding suit is categorically different from neglect. At minimum, disputed facts on diligence and causation require remand.

### C. Alternatively, § 108(c) preserved the action.

The airline's petition on [date], before the two years expired on [date], automatically stayed commencement of this action against it. 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(1). When "applicable nonbankruptcy law" fixes an unexpired period for suing the debtor, the period does not expire until the later of its end, "including any suspension of such period occurring on or after the commencement of the case," or 30 days after notice of the stay's termination or expiration. *Id.* § 108(c)(1)–(2).

Article 35 is nonbankruptcy law fixing a period to bring a civil action. Section 108(c)(2) supplies a definite federal extension and requires no equitable discretion. Appellant received notice on [date] and sued on [date], within 30 days.

The provisions can be harmonized. Article 35 requires timely suit but does not say that time runs out while federal law forbids filing, and Article 35(2) directs the Court to forum law. Reading the treaty to extinguish a claim during the stay would penalize obedience to federal law and let the carrier's own filing defeat liability. Nothing in Article 35 clearly requires that result. The judgment should be reversed.
